buddha_life:
Every other node on this page begins from the teaching; this one sets out **the person who taught it** and the situation in which he taught — without it, the reader cannot judge what “[[dependent_origination|dependent origination]]” was arguing against.

**The person** Śākyamuni, of the Gautama clan, given name Siddhārtha, born among the Śākya people of what is now the border between southern Nepal and Uttar Pradesh in India. The early scriptures record extremely little: birth into a noble family, leaving the city and going forth at twenty-nine (or, by one account, between twenty-nine and thirty), awakening at Bodh Gaya at thirty-five, thereafter forty or fifty years of wandering and teaching in Magadha, Kosala and other lands, and entry into nirvāṇa at Kuśinagara at eighty. **Stock formulas such as “[[reading_a_sutra|Thus have I heard]], at one time the Buddha was staying at…” provide almost no biographical detail** — the accounts of his life (conception by a white elephant, the four excursions, six years of austerities) were mostly formed in later ages, and their literary and symbolic elements far exceed their historical material, so this page treats “biography” and “teaching” separately.

**Dates** Three chronologies for the Buddha's birth and death stand side by side: the Southern tradition (624–544 BCE), the Chinese tradition (565–486 BCE), and modern scholarship (c. 480–400 BCE). This page uniformly counts from “c. 5th century BCE” and adopts none of the three; the three differ by a century, and precisely this century is the key interval for judging which contents of the Āgamas belong to the earliest layer.

**India at the time** The Buddha was a contemporary of the **six non-Buddhist teachers** (Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, Ajita Kesakambala, Pakudha Kaccāyana, and Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta), and two currents dominated the intellectual world:

- **The Brahmanical tradition of sacrifice and the identity of self and brahman** — with Vedic authority, sacrificial ritual and caste as the order of things, holding that there is a permanent “self” (ātman) identical with “brahman”;
- **The negating and ascetic current of the śramaṇas** — the Jains, the Lokāyata materialists, and the various teachers of “wrong views” who did not believe in causality, did not believe in giving, and did not believe in another world.

Buddhism stands between the two: it opposes the authority of sacrifice and the absoluteness of caste (“not by caste, but by action”), and it opposes a permanent self ([[anatta|non-self]]), yet it affirms the reality of good and evil karma and of rebirth — this is precisely why it was regarded as heterodox by the Brahmins and as theistic by the teachers of “wrong views”. [[dependent_origination|Dependent origination]] and the [[five_aggregates|five aggregates]] can be read out only against the background of these two opponents: the former replaces “brahman” as the principle explaining the world and liberation, the latter replaces “self” as the unit for the analysis of experience.

**Why this stands on its own** The two confusions most common among beginners — “did the Buddha really say these things?” and “what exactly did the Buddha say, and what did he not say?” — both require first a coordinate of time, place and person. **Criteria of distinction** (as used on this page, not a settled conclusion of scholarship): **belongs to the early record** — found in both the Pali Nikāyas and the Chinese four Āgamas, and tied to a concrete teaching context by the teaching formula “Thus have I heard, at one time the Buddha was staying at…”; **belongs to later biography** — found only in biographical literature and commentaries and not in the Āgamas of the two transmissions (such as the details of conception by a white elephant, the four excursions, and six years of austerities); **still undetermined** — such as the dates of the Buddha's birth and death, and the historicity of certain accounts of supernatural transformation. This criterion may also be put thus: **what is judged is “which class of literature it appears in”, not “whether it is credible”**.

This page undertakes no source criticism; it only distinguishes “what belongs to the early record, what belongs to later biography, and what scholarship still leaves undetermined”.
reading_a_sutra:
An index can indicate where a concept stands; it cannot read the scripture for the reader. This node sets out only **the few things one must recognize on the way in**, so that a reader can open a scripture without being stopped by its conventions.

**1. Look at the opening** “Thus have I heard, at one time, the Buddha was staying at …, together with a great assembly of monks” is the fixed opening of most sūtras: “Thus” refers to the content transmitted; “I have heard” marks it as the transmission formula spoken by Ānanda at the [[councils|council]]; “at one time” is the habit of not recording a specific date (India had a weak tradition of official history, so Buddhist sūtras are not dated to a year); “the Buddha was staying at … together with a great assembly of monks” indicates the place of teaching and the audience — and **the composition of the audience often indicates the nature of the teaching**: to the renunciant assembly, the [[three_trainings|three trainings in ethics, concentration and wisdom]]; to the lay assembly, giving, the precepts and rebirth in heaven; to the bodhisattva assembly, the six perfections (giving, the precepts, patience, effort, meditation and wisdom) and tathāgatagarbha.

**2. Look at the divisions** Chinese exegesis commonly divides a sūtra into three parts: the **introduction** (the reason for the teaching: who asked, and on what account; the introduction is further divided into the “common introduction” and the “specific introduction”: **the common introduction is the six accomplishments** — the six items of faith, hearing, time, master, place and assembly being complete, which is common to all sūtras; the **specific introduction** is the occasion for arising peculiar to this sūtra), the **main body** (the teaching itself) and the **conveyance section** (entrustment and transmission). With a long unfamiliar sūtra, find these three sections first; the substance is usually in the middle. Exegetical divisions differ from school to school (Tiantai and Huayan each have their own), but the three-part frame is shared.

**3. First establish which translation is in hand** One and the same text often has several translations, and they differ considerably:

- The *Lotus Sūtra* has Kumārajīva's translation (the standard one) and variant translations by Dharmarakṣa and others; Kumārajīva's text is smooth and became the basis of all later commentaries;
- The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* has the earlier portion translated by Dharmakṣema under the Northern Liang and the later *Supplementary Portion*; **the question of whether the icchantika can attain Buddhahood turns precisely on the difference between the earlier and the later portions** (see [[icchantika|the icchantika]]);
- Treatises are the same: the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* has Paramārtha's old translation and Xuanzang's new one, with different terms, so in reading commentaries one must establish which line is being followed.

**4. See which basket it belongs to** Sūtra (spoken by the Buddha, including later compilation), vinaya (monastic procedure and precepts) and treatise (the scholastics' arrangement and debate of the teaching) have different conventions: sūtras emphasize suitability to capacity and sequence, treatises emphasize definition and argument. **A treatise cannot be read as a sūtra** — a treatise first sets up terms and then gives definitions, forcing out its definitions through question and answer (see [[abhidharma|Abhidharma]]); read in the manner of a sūtra, in search of “what the Buddha said”, one cannot get into it.

**5. First read an introduction, then the text** This page and most reference works can provide position and background, but **the reading of the scripture must rely on a lineage of teachers or a reliable commentary**. The practical order is: first see the place of this sūtra in the system and the exposition of the relevant node on this page, then read an old commentary (such as Tiantai's *Fahua Wenju*) or a modern introduction, and finally read the text itself.

**One last point** Scriptures commonly interleave “provisional statements” and “definitive statements” (for example, “the icchantika cannot attain Buddhahood” and “all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature” coexist in the same sūtra). On encountering contradictory passages, do not rush to decide who is right and who is wrong, but ask first: **to whom is this said, and at what level** — this is both the ground on which doctrinal classification is established and what is meant in the [[four_reliances|four reliances]] by “rely on the sūtras of definitive meaning, not on those of provisional meaning”.
simile_index:
Buddhist literature is exceptionally good at using similes, and **most similes come from the scriptures and treatises themselves** — they were not made up by later people to make things easier to understand. No exposition on this page invents a simile of its own (a simile that does not come from a scripture or treatise has no source, and would also pass off one school's solution as “what Buddhism says”); this node gathers the tradition's own similes in one place, for two purposes: to enter by simile on a first reading, and to trace a simile back to its source text on a deeper reading.

**1. Explaining that [[continuity|continuity]] is neither permanent nor annihilated**

- **The lamp flame continuing** — one oil lamp passes its light to the next: the earlier flame is not the later flame, and yet the later flame does not arise from another. Used to say that [[samsara|saṃsāra]] is a “continuity” and not the migration of a substance; the Yogācāra description of [[alaya|ālaya-consciousness]] holding seeds as “rolling on like a torrent” is the technical form of the same image (see [[flame_analogy|the lamp-transmission analogy]], [[continuity|continuity]]). Sources: the lamp similes in the *Saṃyukta-āgama*; *Cheng Weishi Lun*, fascicle 3, “rolling on like a torrent”.

**2. Explaining mutual dependence without substance**

- **Two bundles of reeds leaning on each other** — two bundles of reeds stand only by leaning against each other; remove one and both fall. Used to say that consciousness and name-and-form depend on each other; this is the tersest scriptural formulation of “continuity without a self” (see [[link_namarupa|name-and-form]]). Source: *Saṃyukta-āgama*, fascicle 12, and elsewhere.

**3. Explaining that the mind is defiled but not inherently defiled**

- **Guest and dust** — “guest” is a passing traveller and “dust” is floating motes: defilements are like a guest and like dust, not the essence of the mind. This simile is the scriptural proof for the doctrine of [[pure_mind|the intrinsically pure mind]]. Source: *Śrīmālādevī Sūtra*.
- **Mirror and reflections** — a mirror can reflect all things without itself being defiled. **Here note carefully**: Yogācāra uses the “great mirror wisdom” to speak of the Buddha's wisdom (see [[four_wisdoms|the four wisdoms]]), while the Prajñāpāramitā line uses “like an image in a mirror” to say that all dharmas are unattainable — **the same image is used in opposite ways by the two lines**, and the two must not be conflated. Sources: *Cheng Weishi Lun*, fascicle 10; the “ten similes” of the Prajñāpāramitā cited in *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 6.

**4. Explaining the doing of karma and the receiving of its fruit without a self**

- **The chariot** — a chariot is only a designation for wheel, axle, shaft, yoke and the other parts; apart from the parts there is no “chariot”; so too “I” is only a designation for the [[five_aggregates|five aggregates]] (see [[pudgala|the provisional self]]). Source: *Milindapañha* (the dialogue of Nāgasena and King Milinda).
- **Fire and fuel** — fire burns in dependence on fuel, and when the fuel is exhausted the fire goes out; used to say that the doer of karma and the receiver of its fruit are neither one nor different (see [[karma_ownership|the ownership of karma]]). Source: *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 12.61 and elsewhere.

**5. Explaining that the dharma-doors have levels**

- **The city of nirvāṇa has three gates** — one and the same city has three gates by which it may be entered; the gates differ but the city does not; used to say that emptiness, signlessness and wishlessness are three faces of one dharma (see [[three_doors|the three doors of liberation]]). Source: *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 20.
- **The raft** — a raft is used to cross a river, and once across it should be abandoned, not carried on one's back; “the Dharma itself is still to be abandoned, how much more what is not the Dharma.” Source: the *Raft Simile Sūtra* of the *Madhyama-āgama* (the Pali *Alagaddūpama Sutta*, *Majjhima Nikāya* 22, has the same simile).
- **Five flavours** — milk, curds, fresh butter, clarified butter, ghee, deepening in succession; used to say that the teachings proceed from the shallow to the profound and that doctrinal classification has levels (Tiantai's “five flavours” doctrinal classification takes this simile; see [[wushi_bajiao|the five periods and eight teachings]]). Source: *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 8, “Chapter on the Tathāgata-nature”.

**6. Explaining that ultimate reality is unattainable**

- **The ten similes** — like an illusion, like a mirage, like the moon in water, like space, like an echo, like the city of the gandharvas, like a dream, like a shadow, like an image in a mirror, like a magical creation. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 6, cites these ten similes at length in order to say that all dharmas are without own-nature (see [[emptiness|emptiness]]). Source: the Prajñāpāramitā scriptures cited in *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 6.

**7. Explaining the limits of language**

- **The finger and the moon** — the finger can point out the moon, but the moon is not in the finger; take the finger as the moon and one loses both the moon and the finger. Used to say that the scriptures are the pointing finger that expresses, not the moon that is expressed (see [[four_reliances|the four reliances]], “rely on the meaning, not on the words”). Source: *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
- **Panning gold from sand** — to pick true gold out of sand, not to take all the sand. Used to say that monastics should sift the teachings for what is true (see [[historical_layers|the method of textual stratification]] and the discernment meant by the four reliances). Source: *Samayabhedoparacanacakra*.

**On how this node was verified** Every simile and source listed above was compared item by item against the Chinese canon (CBETA), the Pali canon (SuttaCentral) and the text of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*; where a fascicle number could not be determined it is not given, and only the scripture title is offered. If the edition seen by a reader numbers the fascicles differently, the canonical text should be taken as authoritative — **the reliability of a simile lies not on this page, but in the source text to which it points**.
southern_tradition:
The transmission of Theravāda Buddhism in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia (Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia), grounded in the Pali canon; it is the only Buddhist tradition today that continues **an earlier form**.

**The composition of the three baskets** (by which the reader may judge which basket a text belongs to; the *Visuddhimagga* is not to be mistaken for a sūtra):

- **Vinaya-piṭaka** — the *Suttavibhaṅga* (item-by-item explanation of the Pāṭimokkha of monks and nuns), the *Khandhaka* (monastic procedure and institutions), and the *Parivāra* (a summary arrangement);
- **Sutta-piṭaka** — the five Nikāyas: the *Dīgha Nikāya*, *Majjhima Nikāya*, *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, *Aṅguttara Nikāya* and *Khuddaka Nikāya*;
- **Abhidhamma-piṭaka** — the seven treatises: the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, *Vibhaṅga*, *Dhātukathā*, *Puggalapaññatti*, *Kathāvatthu*, *Yamaka* and *Paṭṭhāna*.

The *Visuddhimagga* is a **commentarial treatise** composed by Buddhaghosa; it belongs to the arrangement of the Sutta-piṭaka and is not one of the seven treatises of the Abhidhamma-piṭaka.

**Establishment of the text** The Pali canon was first preserved orally in Sri Lanka and, according to the *[[doc_51|Dīpavaṃsa]]*, was first committed to writing in the 1st century BCE (in the time of King Vaṭṭagāmaṇī); thereafter came the systematic commentaries of Buddhaghosa (5th century), whose *[[doc_35|Visuddhimagga]]* organized the whole of practice under the three trainings of ethics, concentration and wisdom, and became the standard treatise of the southern tradition.

**Divergence from the northern transmission** The southern tradition does not recognize the Mahāyāna sūtras or the later treatises, and therefore has no tathāgatagarbha, no ālaya-consciousness, and no ten-stage bodhisattva system; but it preserves **the details of the precepts and of meditation with exceptional completeness** — for example the complete method of practice in the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta*, the analysis of the factors of the four dhyānas and eight concentrations, and the sixteen stages of insight knowledge are all more specific than in the northern transmission.

**The modern insight movement** In the 20th century the southern tradition developed a vipassanā tradition aimed at laypeople: Mahasi Sayadaw, U Ba Khin and S. N. Goenka in Myanmar, and Ajahn Chah and the forest tradition in Thailand, among others, simplified the originally monastic meditation methods into courses that could be practised intensively over short periods and spread them throughout the world. **This is the most successful instance of the modern dissemination of Buddhism**, and it has in turn influenced meditative practice in Chinese Buddhism and in the West.

**A common mirror-image misreading** Calling the southern tradition “Hīnayāna” is a sectarian position and is also inaccurate: the southern tradition itself calls itself only the Theravāda or the Vibhajyavāda system, and its goals of practice and its doctrinal system are not “lesser” — what it preserves is the complete practice of the three trainings and the Four Noble Truths, and only its stance on doctrinal classification differs.
development_layer:
**Criterion**: whatever adds, on the basis of the early layer, either a “systematic organization of doctrine” or an “expansion in time, space and ontology” belongs to the developmental layer — the former, for example the dharma-number system of the Abhidharma, the five categories and seventy-five dharmas of the Sarvāstivāda, and the eight consciousnesses and three natures of Yogācāra; the latter, for example the Buddhas of the ten directions, pure lands in other directions, tathāgatagarbha, and the tantras.

The Mahāyāna [[bodhisattva_path|bodhisattva path]], the Buddhas of the ten directions, the [[pure_land|Land of Bliss]], tathāgatagarbha, the Yogācāra and Madhyamaka systems, the tantras, and systems of doctrinal classification.

This layer is characterized by the addition of “expansion in time and space” and “ontological affirmation”.

- Expansion: the horizon of early Buddhism centered on a single Buddha, Śākyamuni, and the present world; the developmental layer introduces the Buddhas of the ten directions, many Buddhas across many aeons, and pure lands in other directions (the Land of Bliss), and Buddhist cosmology unfolds from this;
- Affirmation: the early layer emphasizes the negative formulation of “non-self” and “absence of own-nature”; the developmental layer introduces affirmative formulations such as tathāgatagarbha and Buddha-nature, providing an ontological basis for the attainment of Buddhahood;
- Organization: Madhyamaka and Yogācāra established complete philosophical systems, while systems of doctrinal classification arranged the many scriptures into an order.

Chronologically, the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras (ca. 1st century BCE–2nd century CE) are the starting point of the developmental layer, followed in order by Madhyamaka (2nd–3rd century), the tathāgatagarbha scriptures (3rd–5th century), Yogācāra (4th–5th century), the tantras (after the 7th century), and the Chinese systems of doctrinal classification (6th–8th century).
translation_history:
The translation of Buddhist texts into Chinese spanned about eight hundred years (2nd–8th century) and can be divided into four stages. **The basis of the periodization is “the chief translator and the translation style”**: in the early period most translators were foreign monks working from oral recitation, and matching meanings (ko-i) was unavoidable; the Kumārajīva period established the standard of free translation that conveys the sense; the period from Paramārtha to Xuanzang is the dividing line between the “old translation” and the “new translation”; thereafter state translation bureaus and school commentaries predominated. The four stages are therefore both a chronological division and a periodization of translation method — **this is the backbone of the development of Chinese Buddhism**, since the sequence of the Chinese schools is almost the sequence of scripture translation.

**I. Early translation (Eastern Han to Western Jin, 2nd–3rd century)** An Shigao translated works on meditation and abhidharma (the *Ānāpānasmṛti-sūtra* and others, belonging to the [[sarvastivada|Sarvāstivāda]] system), and Lokakṣema translated the Prajñāpāramitā (the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, 179) — **the two lines of meditation and prajñā were transmitted in parallel from the beginning**. Translators of this period were mostly foreign monks working largely from oral recitation; their style was plain and abounded in [[yichang|matching meanings (ko-i)]].

**II. Kumārajīva and the period between the old and new translations (4th–5th century)** Kumārajīva (arrived in Chang'an in 401, translated 401–413) produced the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Zhong lun), *Śataśāstra*, *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, *Lotus Sūtra* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka), *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, and others, and was renowned for “free translation that conveys the sense”, so that Madhyamaka and prajñā learning truly entered China; thereafter Paramārtha (6th century) translated the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other works, forming the “old translation” of Yogācāra.

**III. Xuanzang's new translation (7th century)** Xuanzang (returned to China in 645, translated 645–664) produced the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (646–648), the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Jushe lun, 651–654), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (660–663), and others, seventy-five works in more than thirteen hundred fascicles in all, and with the *Cheng Weishi Lun* (659) conflated the commentaries of ten masters into a single translation, forming the “new translation” of Yogācāra. **The difference between the new and old translations is not merely verbal** — the same treatise can be read in a completely different way as regards terminology and doctrine, and this is the reason the Shelun masters and the Faxiang school took separate paths.

**IV. Yijing and the translation of esoteric texts (7th–8th century)** Yijing (traveled west 671–695, translated after his return) supplemented the Vinaya with the *Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya*; Śubhakarasiṃha (who translated the *Mahāvairocanābhisambodhi-tantra* in 724), Vajrabodhi and Amoghavajra translated the tantras, and Tang esoteric Buddhism was established. After this, with the Huichang persecution (845), translation work was interrupted.

**The explanatory power of this periodization** Setting the founding dates of the schools beside the dates of translation reveals a high degree of synchrony: the translation of the Prajñāpāramitā → the Sanlun school; of the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* → the Tiantai school; of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* → the Huayan school; of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Cheng Weishi Lun* → the Shelun masters and the Faxiang school; of the tantras → the Esoteric school. **The sectarian history of Chinese Buddhism is to a large extent a history of scripture translation.**
precepts:
The core of the [[vinaya|Vinaya school]]: the [[five_precepts|five precepts]], the ten wholesome courses of action, the full ordination precepts, and so on.

The precepts received differ between laypeople and monastics: laypeople receive the five precepts (not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not lying, not drinking alcohol); novices receive the ten precepts; monks receive two hundred and fifty precepts (according to the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*), nuns three hundred and forty-eight; the bodhisattva precepts are taken separately, according to the ten major and forty-eight minor precepts of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.

What is obtained by receiving the precepts is called the **essence of the precepts** — the capacity induced in body and mind at the time of ordination that can prevent and stop evil action; its essential nature is described differently by the various schools: the Sarvāstivāda posits an “unmanifest material form” (see [[rupa|material dharmas]]), while the Sautrāntika and Yogācāra do not allow it to be a material dharma, and describe it either as a seed of volition or as a seed of mind. This divergence directly determines the explanation of “how the precepts continue”.

The function of the precepts lies in “preventing wrong and stopping evil” and in “serving as the basis for concentration and wisdom”: the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* holds that “the precepts are the cause of concentration and wisdom”; without the precepts, concentration is not firm and wisdom is not genuine. The precepts are therefore not a preparatory stage of practice but a foundation running through the whole of it.

The practical difficulty of the Vinaya school lies in the adaptation of the precepts to their times: the rules arose in a particular time and place in India, and how to adapt them to Chinese customs without violating the essence of the precepts was the central task of successive vinaya masters. It is also the origin of the doctrine of “vinaya according to locality” (the adjustment of precepts to local custom).
one_mind_3000:
A single moment of mind contains in full the three thousand worlds. The classic statement in fascicle 5 of the *[[doc_39|Mohe Zhiguan]]*: “Now, one mind contains the ten dharma-realms, and one dharma-realm in turn contains the ten dharma-realms, [making] a hundred dharma-realms; one realm contains thirty kinds of world, so a hundred dharma-realms contain three thousand kinds of world. These three thousand are in a single moment of mind: if there is no mind, that is all; but as soon as there is the slightest mind, it contains the three thousand.”

The calculation of the three thousand: the ten dharma-realms (the six ordinary realms plus the four noble realms) × the ten dharma-realms (each realm again containing the ten realms) = a hundred dharma-realms; a hundred dharma-realms × the ten suchnesses (**characteristic** = the outward manifest form, **nature** = the inward essential nature, **substance** = the quality of the entity itself, **power** = functional potential, **activity** = the activity of producing, **cause** = the direct cause, **condition** = the auxiliary condition, **effect** = the effect produced, **retribution** = the retribution in later lives, **the ultimate equality of beginning and end** = both the initial characteristic and the final retribution return to ultimate reality) = a thousand suchnesses; a thousand suchnesses × the three kinds of world (the world of the five aggregates, the world of sentient beings, and the world of the land) = the three thousand worlds.

The key lies in the relation between “a single moment” and “the three thousand.” The *Mohe Zhiguan* states explicitly: “It is not said that one mind comes first and all dharmas afterwards; nor is it said that all dharmas come first and one mind afterwards” — it is not that the mind generates the three thousand (vertically), nor that the mind contains the three thousand all at once (horizontally), but that “the mind alone is all dharmas, and all dharmas are the mind.” “The three thousand” is therefore a synonym for “all dharmas,” and one need not fixate on the number; its essential spirit is “inherent inclusion” — the ordinary person's present single moment of mind is already complete in possessing everything, with no need to seek outside.

The scriptural basis of the doctrine is the *[[doc_12|Avataṃsaka Sūtra]]*, “Chapter on the Sovereignty of the Yāma Heaven Palace”: “Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — these three are without distinction”; but “three thousand realms in a single moment of mind” itself is a contemplation unique to Tiantai.
kaifozhijian:
The cardinal teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*: opening, showing, awakening to, and entering the Buddha's insight.

The sūtra says that the sole great cause for the Buddha's appearance in the world is to lead sentient beings to “open the Buddha's insight, show the Buddha's insight, awaken to the Buddha's insight, and enter the Buddha's insight.” Tiantai takes this as the reason for judging the *Lotus* to be purely perfect — the *Lotus* sets forth no expedient device apart from opening the provisional to reveal the real, but speaks only of the Buddha's true intent.

Each of the four words has its own meaning, corresponding to stages of practice: **opening** — breaking through ignorance and opening up the insight that is inherently possessed (as when a cataract is removed and one sees things); **showing** — pointing out the essence and characteristics of the insight so that it becomes clear (as when an object is shown to a person); **awakening** — causing sentient beings to comprehend and realize it for themselves (as when a person sees an object and recognizes it); **entering** — realizing and entering the ultimate, merging with the Buddha's insight (as when a person arrives where the object is).

“Opening” has a double meaning: first, “opening away,” that is, removing sentient beings' attachment to provisional teachings; second, “opening up,” that is, revealing the Buddha's insight that is inherently possessed. “Opening the Buddha's insight” therefore corresponds structurally to “all sentient beings possess the [[buddha_nature|Buddha-nature]]”: the insight is not added from outside but is inherently possessed and obscured.

Relation to the “[[six_identities|six identities]]”: “opening the Buddha's insight” is the cardinal teaching of the doctrinal classification, while the “six identities” are the stages of practice; the former explains the nature of the goal, the latter the position of attainment.
